longo.nar: In January, the industry's main layoff tracker published a forecast for this year. Eight thousand and twenty five jobs. That was the number the whole industry planned around.
By the end of July the same tracker, run by the same person, using the same method, was forecasting fourteen thousand two hundred and fifty nine.
That is a jump of seventy-eight per cent. Not year over year. Within a single year, about a single year.
Almost nobody covered the revision. Everybody covered the total. Those are very different stories, and only one of them tells you where things are going.
A total is a photograph. It tells you where the number stands on the day somebody wrote it down.
A revision is a direction. It tells you which way the estimate has been moving, and how fast, and that survives the next headline.

longo.kicker: So this is not a doom video
longo.nar: So this is not a video about how bad things are. It is a video about how to read a number that keeps changing.
Three things. How the tracker actually works. Where the revisions have gone so far. And, at the end, what none of this predicts.
One thing up front. I will not give you a final figure for this year. Nobody has one, and a quarter is still open.
What I will give you is the mechanism, so the next revision is something you can read instead of something that lands on you.

longo.sub: because it is not a census
longo.nar: Start with the tracker itself. Because it is not what most people assume it is.
The tracker is not a census of the industry. Nobody has that. It is a ledger of publicly reported job losses, assembled from announcements, filings and confirmed reporting.
It is maintained by Amir Satvat, a business development director at Tencent Games, and it is the number the trade press cites when it cites a number.
It has two columns that behave completely differently, and mixing them is where most confusion starts.
Confirmed. As of late July, nine thousand seven hundred and eighty one people. These are counted, named events. This column only ever goes up.
Projected. Fourteen thousand two hundred and fifty nine by year end. This is the estimate, and this column moves in both directions in principle.
In practice, this year, it has gone one way. And the reason is structural, not editorial.
Between the two most recent updates the confirmed column added three hundred and seventeen people. Three per cent, in a matter of weeks.
Here is why that matters. A layoff happens on a Tuesday. It gets confirmed when somebody reports it, which can be weeks later.
So the confirmed column is always behind reality by however long confirmation takes. Not because it is sloppy. Because that is what confirming means.
Which means the confirmed number is a floor. The real figure on any given day is that number or higher, never lower.
Now let us look at what the last few years actually did.
Here are the confirmed totals, year by year, from the same tracker. And the shape is not the one most people carry in their head.
Twenty twenty-two, eight thousand five hundred. Twenty twenty-three, ten thousand five hundred. Twenty twenty-four, fifteen thousand six hundred and thirty one.
Then twenty twenty-five came in at nine thousand one hundred and ninety seven. A real drop, and a lot of people read that as the end of it.

longo.sub: already past three of those four
longo.nar: This year has already passed twenty twenty-two, twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-five on confirmed alone. With a quarter still to run.
The peak still stands. Twenty twenty-four was worse than what this year is projected to reach, and saying otherwise would be overselling it.
But what changed is the shape. Last year looked like a recovery. This year makes it look more like a pause in the middle of something longer.

longo.sub: is the number to sit with
longo.nar: And if you add the five years together, the projection lands near sixty thousand people. That is the number I would sit with, not any single year.
Single years can be argued about. One studio closing can move a year. The five-year sum is much harder to explain away.

longo.preco: these are not the same people
longo.nar: One caution before we go on. Sixty thousand job losses is not sixty thousand different people. Some are counted more than once across years.

longo.sub: so I will not invent it
longo.nar: Nobody publishes how many. So I am not going to estimate it, and you should be sceptical of anybody who does.
Next, the part that changes who this is actually happening to.
This is the part that reframes the whole thing for me. North America and Europe account for ninety-five per cent of all games industry layoffs in this dataset. Not most of them. Almost all of them.
The United States alone is forty-eight per cent of this year's total. Canada adds seventeen. Europe adds thirty.

longo.sub: five per cent for everywhere else
longo.nar: Which leaves about five per cent for the entire rest of the world. Japan, Korea, China, India, Brazil, all of it, inside that five.
Now hold on before you draw the obvious conclusion, because this number cuts in two directions and only one of them gets said out loud.
The first reading is the popular one. Western studios are contracting, and development is moving to cheaper places. That reading is not wrong.
The second reading is about the ledger itself. It counts what is publicly reported, and public reporting of layoffs is far denser in English-language markets than anywhere else.

longo.sub: in a market with less trade press
longo.nar: A studio that shrinks quietly in a market with less trade press coverage may simply not enter this dataset at all. Not hidden. Just never written down.

longo.sub: is concentration, how much is visibility
longo.nar: So how much of that ninety-five per cent is real concentration, and how much is visibility? I do not know, and neither does anybody quoting it at you.

longo.preco: it is a ceiling for the west
longo.nar: What I can say is narrower. For western developers, this figure is not an overstatement. Whatever the rest of the world's true number is, it does not subtract from theirs.

longo.sub: and it is still bad news
longo.nar: That is the honest version of the geography claim. It is still bad news for the people in it, and it is a weaker claim than the headline makes.

longo.sub: and why it keeps going up
longo.nar: Which brings us back to the revision, and why it has only moved one way.
The intuitive explanation for a seventy-eight per cent upward revision is that things got much worse than expected between January and July. That may be part of it. It is not the whole thing.
longo.cap: Why the direction is not random

longo.sub: of how the forecast is built
longo.nar: Part of it is arithmetic, built into how any forecast of this kind works. And once you see it, the revisions stop feeling like shocks.

longo.preco: has almost no year in it
longo.nar: A forecast published in January is built on almost no data from the year it is forecasting. It leans on last year, and last year was the low one.
So it starts low. Not pessimistically or optimistically. By construction.
Every month after that adds real confirmed events, and confirmed events only ever add. There is no mechanism for a confirmed layoff to un-happen.

longo.sub: walks upward as the year fills in
longo.nar: So the estimate walks upward as the year fills in. It would do that even in a year that turned out completely normal.

longo.sub: the revision is not the alarm
longo.nar: Which is why the size of the revision, on its own, is not the alarm people read it as. Some upward drift is the method, not the message.

longo.preco: faster or slower than the drift
longo.nar: The real question is whether it is drifting faster than normal. And that you answer by comparing the same month across years, not by staring at one jump.
And I am flagging clearly: that mechanism is my reading of how the forecast is built. It is not a claim the tracker publishes.

longo.sub: because it changes what you trust
longo.nar: I say it out loud because you should hold it more loosely than the counts. The counts are sourced. This is an explanation of them.
So what actually survives when you strip all the framing off?
It does not predict where this year lands. A quarter is open, and one large closure can move the total by a thousand people in an afternoon.
longo.cap: What this does and does not predict

longo.nar: It does not tell you which studio is next. Nobody who tells you that knows, and the ones who claim to are selling something.
It does not measure hiring at all. This is a one-sided ledger. A year with high layoffs and high hiring looks identical here to one with neither.
And the confirmed column is a floor, not a total. What is not publicly reported is not in it, and there is no way to know how much that is.
So what does it actually support? Two things, and both are narrower than the headlines built on them.
The direction the revisions have moved. The five-year floor of roughly sixty thousand reported losses. And that the reported ones are concentrated in two regions.
That is enough to make a career decision with. It is not enough to make a prediction with, and the difference matters.
If you work in this industry, the useful read is not the total. It is that the estimate has moved up every time it has been touched this year.

longo.kicker: And if you are outside it
longo.nar: If you are outside it, the useful read is different again. This is what a sector looks like while it repricies labour, and the counting lags the event.
Neither of those makes a headline. Both of them are more useful than one.
Last part. What I would actually watch from here.
When the next update lands, do not read the total first. Read what the projection was before it, and what it is now.
longo.cap: What to watch instead of the total

longo.nar: The gap between those two is the signal. The total is just where the gap happens to have arrived.
Three numbers, thirty seconds. The previous projection. The new one. And the confirmed column at both dates.
If the projection jumps and the confirmed column barely moves, the model changed its mind. That is worth attention.
If both move together, the year is simply filling in as expected. Less dramatic, and much more common.
That distinction is completely invisible in any headline about the total, and it takes half a minute to check.
One more habit worth having. Compare the same month across years. July to July tells you something. July to January tells you almost nothing.
The tracker and the reporting are both linked below. Go and look, because this is a number you will see quoted badly all year.
In the next video I want to do the other half of this ledger. What the hiring side actually shows, and why it is much harder to count.
Because a ledger with only one side answers half a question, and half a question is how you end up sure about the wrong thing.

short.nar: In January the games layoff forecast for this year was eight thousand and twenty five.
By July, same tracker, same method: fourteen thousand two hundred and fifty nine.
Seventy-eight per cent higher. Same year. Six months apart.
Everyone reported the total. Almost nobody reported the revision.
A total is a photograph. A revision is a direction.
The full breakdown, and why it only moves one way, is on the channel.

# The revision, not the total: reading the 2026 games layoff tracker

## TITULO
Gaming Layoffs 2026: The Forecast Was Revised Up 78% in Six Months

## DESCRICAO
In January, the ASGC Games Industry Layoffs Tracker forecast 8,025 games industry job losses for 2026. By the end of July, the same tracker — same maintainer, same method — was projecting 14,259. That is a 78% upward revision inside a single year, about that same year.

Almost every outlet covered the total. Almost none covered the revision. A total is a photograph: it tells you where the number stood the day someone wrote it down. A revision is a direction, and a direction survives the next headline.

What the tracker actually is: not a census of the industry, but a ledger of publicly reported job losses, maintained by Amir Satvat, a business development director at Tencent Games. It has two columns that behave very differently. Confirmed — 9,781 people as of late July, up 317 (+3%) from the previous update — counts named, reported events and only ever rises. Projected is the estimate for year end. Confirmation lags the event by however long reporting takes, which makes the confirmed column a floor, never a total.

The five-year picture, confirmed: 2022 around 8,500; 2023 around 10,500; 2024 the peak at 15,631; 2025 down to 9,197. This year has already passed 2022, 2023 and 2025 on confirmed alone, with a quarter still open — though 2024 remains the worst year on record, and saying otherwise oversells it. Across the five years the projection lands near 60,000 reported losses. That total is not 60,000 distinct people; nobody publishes how much overlap there is, so this video does not estimate it.

Geography: North America and Europe account for 95% of the layoffs in this dataset — the US 48%, Canada 17%, Europe 30%. That figure cuts two ways, and the video takes both seriously. Western studios really are contracting; and the ledger counts what is publicly reported, and public reporting of layoffs is far denser in English-language markets. How much of the 95% is concentration and how much is visibility is not knowable from this data.

On why revisions keep moving up: a January forecast is built on almost no data from the year it forecasts, and every month afterwards adds confirmed events that can only add. Some upward drift is the method, not the message. That explanation is flagged in the video as reasoning, not as something the tracker publishes.

And the limits: this predicts no final figure, names no studio, measures no hiring at all, and counts only what was reported.

A question for anyone working in the industry: when the next tracker update lands, does your studio's situation show up in it at all — or is it the kind of quiet contraction that never gets publicly reported? I'm trying to get a sense of how much the ledger misses, and that is the one thing the data cannot tell me.
